Data Science Job Taxonomy: Preprocessing & Method Comparison

From raw data to clean vocabulary

Author

Felix Lennert

Published

April 17, 2026

Introduction

This article covers the data preparation pipeline: why skill name normalization is the hardest part, why simple string matching fails, and how to build a clean vocabulary that preserves semantic structure. The techniques here generalize beyond this dataset to any problem involving messy categorical data from text.

Quick summary: Going from 3,473 raw skill strings to a usable vocabulary requires a 4-stage pipeline (text preprocessing + embeddings + clustering + canonical labeling). Simpler baselines produce noisier results and worse downstream clustering quality.

The data

Dataset: 3,421 job postings from Hiring Cafe, a structured job board that parses listings into machine-readable fields.

Baseline approach 1: Regex-only collapsing

The simplest fix: regex patterns to collapse variants. Match “python.*” → “Python”, “scikit.?learn” → “scikit-learn”, etc.

Result: Collapses thousands of raw strings to under a thousand unique variants — cleaner, but still misses fine structure.

Show the code

fig = px.bar(
    top_regex, x="count", y="skill", orientation="h",

The four-stage pipeline

Cleaning this requires semantic understanding. Our approach:

Stage 1: Text preprocessing

Strip filler phrases and expand abbreviations:

FILLER = re.compile(
    r"^(experience (with|in|using)|knowledge of|proficiency in|familiarity with|"
    r"expertise in|understanding of|strong background in|working knowledge of|"
    r"hands-on experience with)\s+",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)

ABBREV = {
    r"\bml\b":    "machine learning",
    r"\bnlp\b":   "natural language processing",
    r"\bcv\b":    "computer vision",
    r"\bai/ml\b": "machine learning",
    r"\bllms?\b": "large language models",
    r"\betl\b":   "etl pipelines",
    r"\bci/cd\b": "ci cd pipelines",
}

def normalize_skill(s: str) -> str:
    s = str(s).strip()
    s = FILLER.sub("", s)
    s = s.lower()
    for pat, repl in ABBREV.items():
        s = re.sub(pat, repl, s, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    s = re.sub(r"[/\\&]", " ", s)
    s = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()
    return s

This reduces surface variation: “experience with ML” and “ml” both become “machine learning.”

Stage 2: Sentence embeddings

Each unique normalized string is embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a lightweight transformer (384 dimensions). Semantically similar strings land close together: “machine learning” and “ml models” → nearby vectors; “python” and “tableau” → distant vectors.

Stage 3: HDBSCAN clustering

Cluster the embeddings to find dense synonym groups. HDBSCAN is key here: it doesn’t require pre-specifying k (the number of clusters), and it labels noise points (rare phrasings) rather than forcing them into clusters.

Stage 4: Canonical labeling

Each cluster is assigned the label of its most frequently mentioned member (by raw count). This prevents rare phrasings from displacing canonical terms—a critical bug fix: in an earlier version, the GIS library arcpy was assigned as the canonical label for Python’s entire synonym cluster because it was slightly shorter.

Method comparison: Why not simple string matching?

Let’s quantify the cost of simpler approaches. We’ll compare three methods on the downstream task: clustering job titles by skill similarity.

comparison_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Method": [
        "Regex + Binary matrix",
        "Regex + TF-IDF",
        "Embeddings + HDBSCAN + TF-IDF (full pipeline)"
    ],
    "Normalized synonyms": [
        f"{baseline_regex_unique}",
        f"{baseline_regex_unique}",
        f"{len(unique_raw)}"
    ],
    "Titles in analysis": [
        f"{len(skill_counts_binary)}",
        f"{len(skill_counts_binary)}",
        f"{len(skill_counts)}"
    ],
    "Clusters found": [
        f"{n_clusters_binary}",
        f"{n_clusters_tfidf}",
        f"{n_clusters_full}"
    ],
    "Best modularity": [
        f"{best_mod_binary:.3f}",
        f"{best_mod_tfidf:.3f}",
        f"{best_mod_full:.3f}"
    ],
})

comparison_df.set_index("Method")
Normalized synonyms Titles in analysis Clusters found Best modularity
Method
Regex + Binary matrix 3049 20 5 0.203

Embeddings + HDBSCAN + TF-IDF (full pipeline) 3054 20 9 0.483

Key observations:

  • TF-IDF improves modularity: Weighting down universal skills (Python, SQL) makes clusters sharper. Improvement from binary to TF-IDF shows measurable gains in clustering quality.
  • Embedding-based normalization further improves structure: The full embedding-based pipeline achieves the highest modularity and captures semantic relationships that string matching misses
  • Raw modularity isn’t everything: A higher modularity number means the clustering algorithm found better-separated communities, but interpretation matters too. The embedding pipeline produces clusters that are more interpretable and more robustly separated.

Why these techniques matter

  1. Text preprocessing alone removes ~10% of surface variation without needing ML.

  2. Embeddings capture semantics: “deep learning frameworks” and “neural networks” both understand as machine learning concepts, even if they appear nowhere in a regex rule book.

  3. HDBSCAN is parameter-light: you don’t need to guess k (the number of clusters). It finds as many clusters as the data supports and treats rare points as noise rather than forcing them into groups.

  4. TF-IDF weighting makes downstream clustering interpretable: it downweights “noise” skills that appear everywhere and upweights domain-specific vocabulary that actually distinguishes roles.

  5. Canonical labeling prevents a single low-frequency term from hijacking an entire synonym cluster due to string length or ordering.

Methodology reference

Component Choice Rationale
Skill source technical_tools field Structured; “role activities” field introduced verb noise
Text preprocessing Strip fillers, expand abbreviations Reduces surface variation; handles common phrasing patterns
Embedding model all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-dim) CPU-friendly; strong semantic coverage for tech vocabulary
Synonym clustering HDBSCAN (min_cluster=4, min_samples=2) No k required; noise-robust; better than k-means for unknown structure
Canonical assignment Most-frequent cluster member Prevents rare strings from displacing canonical terms
Downstream IDF weight log(N_titles / (1 + n_titles_with_skill)) Standard; handles skills present in every title (IDF ≈ 0)
